lesson.subtitle: Lesson 29 -- Reporting to Senior Partners
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Eduarda | Lesson 29 -- Reporting to Senior Partners

listenings.text: Hi Eduarda, it's James. Quick heads-up: Richard Hale wants a briefing on Lane before the investment committee next Tuesday. He's a senior partner, so he doesn't want the whole story. Start with the bottom line, then give him the two or three key points, and finish with a clear recommendation. Keep the executive summary to one page. And don't hide the cap problem. If something is still outstanding, tell him first, and tell him how we plan to mitigate it. Partners hate surprises in the committee. Good luck.

When you report to senior people, remember that their time is the most expensive thing in the room. Use the pyramid: the answer first, then the reasons, and then the details, but only if they ask. Many junior bankers do the opposite. They tell the story from the beginning, and the partner stops listening after one minute. A good report also separates facts from opinions. Say what happened, and then say what you think. And always end with what you need: a decision, a signature or the green light. If the partner doesn't know what you need, the meeting was not useful.

extra_audio.text: NorthPack accepted a twelve-month escrow, but it offered a cap of fifteen percent. James sent Eduarda a heads-up about a briefing with Richard Hale. Eduarda wrote a one-page executive summary. In the meeting, she started with the bottom line. Then she explained the exposure from the supplier case. Finally, she asked Richard for the green light.
